questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between a "role" and a "feature" in Windows Server, per Lesson 1?
options: A role is a major server function like AD DS or DNS; a feature is a smaller supporting capability a role might need, like .NET Framework or BitLocker Drive Encryption
A feature is a major server function, and a role is a smaller supporting capability a feature might need
Roles and features are two different names for the exact same kind of component, added through two separate wizards
A role can only be installed through Server Manager; a feature can only be installed through PowerShell
Every role requires installing every available feature at the same time
Features are deprecated in modern Windows Server and only roles remain
questions.explain: Lesson 1 defines a role as a major server function (AD DS, DNS, DHCP, File and Storage Services, Web Server/IIS) and a feature as a smaller supporting capability like .NET Framework or BitLocker Drive Encryption, both added through the Add Roles and Features Wizard or Install-WindowsFeature.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B reverses the two definitions entirely — it's the role that's the major server function (AD DS, DNS, etc.) and the feature that's the smaller supporting capability, not the other way around, which is exactly the mix-up Lesson 1 is written to prevent.

questions.prompt: Match each Active Directory structural term from Lesson 2 to what it actually is.
right: A container inside a domain used to apply GPOs and delegate admin rights to a subset of objects
The outer AD boundary — one or more trees sharing a schema and Global Catalog
The real administrative and security boundary in AD, with its own domain controllers and database
One or more domains sharing a contiguous DNS namespace
questions.explain: Lesson 2 defines a domain as the real admin/security boundary with its own domain controllers and database, a tree as domains sharing a contiguous DNS namespace, a forest as the outer boundary sharing a schema and Global Catalog, and an OU as the container used for applying GPOs and delegating admin rights rather than a security boundary of its own.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 3, the standard group-nesting pattern in Active Directory is ________ — Accounts go into Global groups, Global groups go into Domain Local groups, and the Domain Local group gets the Permission.
questions.explain: Lesson 3 names this pattern explicitly: accounts nest into global groups (representing real-world people), global groups nest into domain local groups (which hold the actual permission), and the domain local group is what actually gets granted access to a resource.

questions.prompt: A share `\\FS01\HR` has a share permission of Full Control for the HR-Employees group, but the NTFS permission on the underlying folder is Read for that same group. Per Lesson 4, what is HR-Employees' effective access when connecting over the network?
options: Read only — the more restrictive of the two layers (NTFS) wins over the network
Full Control — the more permissive of the two layers wins
Full Control, because share permissions always override NTFS permissions
No access at all, because conflicting permissions cancel each other out
questions.explain: Lesson 4's "most restrictive wins" rule means that when both NTFS and share permissions apply over the network, Windows grants whichever layer's effective permission is tighter — here that's the NTFS Read permission, not the share's Full Control.

questions.prompt: An OU has Block Inheritance turned on. A GPO linked at the domain level, setting a password policy, is also set to Enforced. Per Lesson 5, does that password policy GPO reach computers in that OU?
options: Yes — Enforced overrides Block Inheritance, because Enforced is a property of the GPO being pushed down that the receiving OU cannot opt out of
No — Block Inheritance always wins over any setting on a higher-level GPO
It depends on whether the GPO was linked before or after Block Inheritance was enabled
No — Enforced and Block Inheritance cancel each other out, so no GPO settings reach the OU at all
questions.explain: Lesson 5 is explicit that Enforced always beats Block Inheritance — Enforced is set on the GPO itself and forces it to apply everywhere below it, even an OU that has turned on Block Inheritance, because the receiving OU has no way to opt out of a GPO-level Enforced setting.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 6, the CIS Benchmarks organize hardening settings into Level 1, basic hardening with minimal impact on normal business function, and Level ________, a stricter "defense in depth" level intended for higher-security environments.
questions.explain: Lesson 6 defines CIS Benchmark Level 1 as basic hardening with minimal functional impact and Level 2 as more aggressive defense-in-depth hardening that can affect compatibility, intended for higher-security environments.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Windows Firewall and Defender, per Lesson 7.
options: Inbound traffic is blocked by default unless a rule explicitly allows it
Outbound traffic is blocked by default unless a rule explicitly allows it
The Public profile is the most restrictive of the three firewall profiles by default
Microsoft Defender Antivirus's real-time protection scans files only when a user manually starts a scan
Cloud-delivered protection lets Defender query Microsoft's cloud threat intelligence for a file its local signatures can't confidently classify
questions.explain: Lesson 7 establishes that inbound traffic is blocked by default unless allowed (outbound is the opposite — allowed by default unless blocked), that Public is the most restrictive profile, and that cloud-delivered protection checks an unclassified file against Microsoft's cloud intelligence rather than waiting for a signature update. Real-time protection scans continuously as files are opened, run, downloaded, or modified — not only during a manual scan.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes what the TPM does for BitLocker, per Lesson 8?
options: It stores and protects the encryption key in hardware, separate from the drive, and validates the boot process before releasing that key
It stores the 48-digit recovery key printed on paper, as a replacement for the hardware-based key
It encrypts individual sensitive files one at a time, rather than the whole volume
It only activates after a login password has already been typed at the Windows logon screen
It is a software-only feature with no dedicated hardware component
It generates a brand-new encryption key every time the machine reboots
questions.explain: Lesson 8 describes the TPM as a dedicated hardware chip that stores BitLocker's encryption key separately from the drive and validates boot integrity, withholding the key if the boot process looks tampered with.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B confuses the TPM with the recovery key it's a backup for — the 48-digit recovery key is a separate, printable backup used specifically when the TPM can't release its hardware-held key, not something the TPM itself stores on paper.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 9, why does reading the Security log specifically require administrator rights, when the Application and System logs don't?
options: The Security log records who logged on, who was created, and who was added to which group — letting a non-admin read it freely would let them map out account activity and privilege assignments
The Security log is encrypted and literally cannot be opened without an administrator password
Microsoft restricts it for licensing reasons unrelated to its content
The Application and System logs are also admin-only; only the Setup log is open to standard users
questions.explain: Lesson 9 explains this is a deliberate design choice — the Security log's contents (logons, account changes, group membership) are sensitive enough that a non-admin who could browse it freely could map out account and privilege activity across the machine.

questions.prompt: Put these three Security-log Event IDs from Lesson 10 in the order a textbook privilege-escalation pattern would actually produce them.
items: 4728 — a member was added to a security-enabled global group
4672 — special privileges assigned to the new logon
questions.explain: Lesson 10 describes this exact sequence as a textbook pattern: an account is created (4720), then added into a privileged group (4728), then logs on with the elevated rights that membership now grants (4672) — an attacker or malicious insider quietly provisioning themselves persistent admin access.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Sysmon, per Lesson 11.
options: Sysmon is installed on Windows by default and requires no separate download
Event ID 1 (Process Create) logs the full command line, process hash, and parent process
Event ID 3 (Network Connection) logs the source/destination IP and port when a process initiates a connection
Event ID 11 (File Create) can catch a file whose creation timestamp was overwritten to look older, i.e. "timestomping"
Sysmon writes its events directly into the same Security log Event Viewer shows for Lesson 10's Event IDs
questions.explain: Lesson 11 is explicit that Sysmon is not installed by default — someone has to download and install it — and that it writes to its own dedicated log under Applications and Services Logs, separate from Security. Event ID 1 captures the full command line, hash, and parent process; Event ID 3 captures network connection details; and Event ID 11 can catch a timestomped file's overwritten creation time.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 12, enabling Object Access auditing only generates events for a given file, folder, or registry key once a matching ________ is also set on that specific object.
questions.explain: Lesson 12 is explicit that Object Access auditing governs access to files, folders, or registry keys, but only once a matching SACL (System Access Control List) is also set on that object — enabling the category alone isn't enough.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 13, `/etc/sudoers` should always be edited with ________ rather than a plain text editor, because it validates the file's grammar before allowing the save.
questions.explain: Lesson 13 explains that visudo opens the file in your normal editor but validates syntax before allowing a save, so a bad edit throws a parse error and never gets written to disk — protecting against a typo that could lock every user out of sudo, including the ability to fix sudoers itself.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes what PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules) actually is, per Lesson 14?
options: A shared framework that programs like login, sudo, su, and sshd all call into for authentication, instead of each implementing password checking itself
A Linux kernel module that replaces the need for a password file entirely
A GUI tool for resetting user passwords on a Linux desktop
A feature exclusive to SSH that has no effect on sudo or login
A cron-based job that periodically rotates user passwords automatically
A firewall utility for blocking repeated failed SSH login attempts
questions.explain: Lesson 14 defines PAM as the shared framework every program needing to verify identity calls into — login, sudo, su, sshd, and passwd all hand authentication off to the shared libpam library rather than implementing their own checks.
questions.distractorExplain: Option F describes fail2ban, not PAM — fail2ban (covered later in Lesson 20) watches logs and bans IPs after repeated failures, while PAM is the authentication framework itself that decides whether a single login attempt succeeds, a distinction Lesson 14 draws clearly.

questions.prompt: `/tmp` shows the permissions above. Per Lesson 15, what does the trailing `t` specifically prevent, given that the directory is already world-writable?
options: It stops any user other than a file's owner (or root) from deleting or renaming that file, even though everyone can write to the directory itself
It stops any user from creating new files in `/tmp` at all
It makes every file inside `/tmp` automatically readable only by its owner
It prevents root from accessing any file inside `/tmp`
questions.explain: Lesson 15 explains that plain write permission on a directory would otherwise let any user delete or rename anyone else's files in that directory — the sticky bit (the trailing `t`) specifically restricts delete/rename to a file's own owner or root, without changing who can create new files there.

questions.prompt: A root-owned cron job runs the script above. Select every true statement about this, per Lesson 16.
options: Any unprivileged user on the box can edit this script, and root will execute their changes the next time the job fires
This is a direct, real privilege-escalation path, not just a theoretical concern
The fix is to make the script's permissions more restrictive, such as `chmod 750` or `chmod 700`
This is fully safe as long as the directory `/opt/scripts` itself is also checked, since a writable directory can let someone replace the file even if the file's own permissions are locked down
systemd timers have the exact same missed-run problem as cron and offer no advantage over it
questions.explain: Lesson 16 treats a world-writable, root-run script as a direct privilege-escalation path and recommends chmod 750 or 700, never 777, while also noting the containing directory needs checking too — a writable directory lets someone replace the file entirely even if the file itself is restricted. systemd timers, unlike cron, support Persistent=true to catch up a run missed while the machine was off, which Lesson 16 presents as a real advantage cron doesn't have.

questions.prompt: Match each access-control term from Lesson 17 to what it actually is.
right: Ubuntu/Debian/SUSE's MAC implementation, using path-based profiles in /etc/apparmor.d/
A second, system-wide policy layer checked after DAC, binding even on root
Standard Linux permissions, controlled at the resource owner's discretion; doesn't apply to root
RHEL/CentOS/Fedora's MAC implementation, labeling processes and files with security contexts
questions.explain: Lesson 17 defines DAC as standard, owner-controlled permissions that root bypasses entirely, and MAC as a second, system-wide layer that even root can't opt out of. SELinux (RHEL family) enforces that layer through security-context labels; AppArmor (Ubuntu/Debian family) enforces it through plain-text, path-based profiles instead.

questions.prompt: A text editor used to modify `/etc/shadow` never logs anything about that specific file. With the watch rule above in place, per Lesson 18, why does `auditd` still catch the change when an application-level log wouldn't?
options: auditd works at the kernel level, watching system calls and file access directly based on configured rules, regardless of whether any application chose to log the action itself
auditd intercepts and rewrites every text editor's own log output before it's written
auditd only works for changes made through `passwd`, not through a generic text editor
auditd requires the text editor to be specifically configured to call an auditd API
questions.explain: Lesson 18 draws exactly this distinction — application logs show only what the software chose to record, while auditd operates at the kernel level and logs matching syscall/file-access events based on a watch rule like `-w /etc/shadow -p wa`, independent of whether the responsible application ever mentions the file itself.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 19's safe rollout order, put these steps for disabling SSH password authentication in the correct sequence.
items: Confirm key-based login already works from a second, still-open SSH session
Run `sshd -t` to check the edited config's syntax
Open a third terminal and confirm a brand-new connection succeeds with keys alone before closing the original sessions
questions.explain: Lesson 19 is explicit about this order because flipping PasswordAuthentication no and restarting sshd from your only open session, without verifying key auth first, is the single most common way administrators lock themselves out — confirming key auth works, syntax-checking, restarting, and then verifying a fresh connection before closing old sessions is what prevents that.

questions.prompt: SSH on a server already requires key-based authentication only (`PasswordAuthentication no`). Select every true statement about why the `sshd` fail2ban jail, per Lesson 20, is still worth keeping enabled.
options: A future misconfiguration that silently re-enables password auth is far less dangerous if fail2ban is already watching
fail2ban isn't SSH-only — the same mechanism can protect any service with a log-matchable failure pattern
Even failed key-authentication attempts and connection floods still clutter logs and consume server resources, which banning the source IP helps control
fail2ban is completely redundant once password authentication is disabled, since there's nothing left to brute-force
questions.explain: Lesson 20 directly rejects the idea that fail2ban becomes redundant once passwords are disabled — it lists defense-in-depth against a future misconfiguration, protection for other log-matchable services beyond SSH, and controlling the noise and resource cost of connection floods as real, ongoing reasons to keep the jail enabled.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes "Patch Tuesday," per Lesson 21?
options: Microsoft's practice of releasing the bulk of its security updates on the second Tuesday of every month, so IT departments can plan around a predictable schedule
A weekly patch cycle that Microsoft runs every Tuesday without exception
The day each month when Microsoft disables all out-of-band patches
A Linux-specific patch cadence used by the Debian family
An informal term for the day attackers release zero-day exploits
A patch testing phase that happens before any patch is made public
questions.explain: Lesson 21 defines Patch Tuesday as Microsoft's long-standing practice of releasing most security updates on the second Tuesday of every month specifically so organizations can plan a predictable testing and deployment process around it.
questions.distractorExplain: Option E confuses Patch Tuesday with "Exploit Wednesday," the informal term Lesson 21 uses for attackers reverse-engineering a freshly released patch within days to build a working exploit — that's a reaction to Patch Tuesday, not Patch Tuesday itself, and it isn't when a brand-new zero-day is released.

questions.prompt: A company has 3,000 laptops, all enrolled in Intune, with most employees working remotely and rarely connecting to the corporate network. Per Lesson 22, would WSUS or Windows Update for Business fit better, and why?
options: Windows Update for Business — it's policy-driven through Intune with no on-premises server required, which fits devices that may never touch the corporate network
WSUS — because it offers deployment rings and deferral periods that WUfB doesn't have
WSUS — because it requires devices to be domain-joined, which Intune-enrolled laptops already are
Neither — cloud-managed devices cannot receive Windows updates of any kind
questions.explain: Lesson 22 is explicit that WUfB fits a cloud-managed fleet enrolled in Intune, especially devices that are remote and may rarely or never touch the corporate network, while WSUS fits a traditional on-premises, domain-joined environment where standing up extra infrastructure makes sense.

questions.code:
sudo apt update
sudo apt upgrade
questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 23, running `apt upgrade` without first running `apt ________` risks working off a stale package index that may not show updates that actually exist.
questions.explain: Lesson 23 explains that `apt update` only refreshes the local package index and installs nothing, while `apt upgrade` installs newer versions of already-installed packages — skipping `update` first means `upgrade` may think there's nothing new even when there is.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about CVE and CVSS, per Lesson 24.
options: A CVE ID is a shared, standardized name that lets a vendor advisory, a scanner report, and a news article all reference the exact same vulnerability
CVSS scores a vulnerability on a scale from 0.0 to 10.0, with Critical covering 9.0-10.0
Base metrics change constantly as new exploit code is published, while Temporal metrics never change
Environmental metrics let an organization adjust a score for how much its own confidentiality, integrity, and availability actually depend on the specific asset
A CVE ID by itself tells you exactly how dangerous a vulnerability is, without needing a CVSS score
questions.explain: Lesson 24 reverses option C's claim — Base metrics describe the vulnerability's intrinsic nature and don't change over time, while Temporal metrics are specifically the ones that change after disclosure, such as whether exploit code now exists. It also states plainly that a CVE ID identifies a vulnerability but doesn't by itself convey severity — that's CVSS's job, which runs 0.0-10.0 with Critical at 9.0-10.0, and Environmental metrics let an organization weight the score to its own asset's exposure and value.

questions.prompt: A phishing macro launches PowerShell with an obfuscated, base64-encoded command that downloads a payload directly into memory, writing nothing to disk. Per Lesson 25, why does this defeat signature-based antivirus while still leaving a trail for EDR?
options: Signature-based AV has no file to hash and raises no alert, but EDR's continuous telemetry still shows the process-tree chain — winword.exe spawning powershell.exe with suspicious arguments, then an outbound connection — as a behavioral signal
Signature-based AV would still catch this because it also inspects memory contents in real time by default
EDR only works on files written to disk, so it would miss this attack as completely as antivirus does
This attack is undetectable by any tool because PowerShell is a trusted Microsoft application
questions.explain: Lesson 25's fileless example is exactly this scenario — antivirus has nothing to hash so it raises nothing, while EDR's continuous telemetry sees the parent-child process chain (winword.exe to powershell.exe to an unfamiliar outbound connection) as a behavioral signal, catching what a static file scan never could.

questions.prompt: Match each endpoint/asset term from Lessons 26 and 28 to what it actually means.
right: A system of record listing every known asset, its owner, OS, patch level, and criticality
Registering a device with the Defender for Endpoint tenant so its sensor starts reporting
Assets that exist and run on a network without being tracked in inventory
A correlated group of related alerts representing one attack story, often across multiple devices
questions.explain: Lesson 26 defines onboarding as registering a device so its Defender for Endpoint sensor starts reporting, and an incident as the correlated group of related alerts representing one attack story. Lesson 28 defines a CMDB as the system of record for every known asset, and shadow IT as whatever a network discovery scan finds that the CMDB has no record of.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 27, `________` is the ClamAV command that pulls down an updated signature database, the same ongoing need any signature-based tool has.
questions.explain: Lesson 27 names `freshclam` specifically as the command that updates ClamAV's signature database, alongside `clamscan -r` for an on-demand recursive scan and the `clamd` daemon for continuous background scanning.

questions.prompt: On `WIN-SRV-04`, the Private and Public Windows Firewall profiles are left with no custom rules at all, just default deny-all-inbound. Per Lesson 29, why is this a deliberate hardening decision rather than an oversight?
options: The server only ever connects to the network as a domain member, so it will never legitimately appear on a Private or Public network — leaving those profiles at default deny is itself a control
Windows Firewall cannot have rules configured on more than one profile at a time
The Private and Public profiles are automatically disabled on any domain-joined server
Default deny-all-inbound is the weakest possible firewall setting and should always be replaced with explicit rules
questions.explain: Lesson 29 explains that WIN-SRV-04, as a domain member, will never legitimately find itself on a Private or Public network, so there's no rule to write for either — leaving them at their already-restrictive default is exactly the right call, not something left unfinished.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 30, put these steps for flipping SELinux from permissive to enforcing on `lnx-app-02` in the correct order.
items: Run `ausearch -m avc -ts recent` to check for existing denials
Run `restorecon -R` to fix any files with the wrong SELinux context
Set `SELINUX=enforcing` in `/etc/selinux/config` so it survives a reboot
questions.explain: Lesson 30 walks this exact order — checking for denials first so flipping enforcement doesn't blindly break the app, fixing mislabeled file contexts before enforcement goes live, enforcing immediately with setenforce 1, and only then making it permanent in the config file so it survives a reboot.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes why Meridian Fabrication's finding 3 — root SSH login and password authentication both enabled on `lnx-db-01` — gets treated differently from finding 1 (unpatched servers), per Lesson 31?
options: Because the exposure represents a potential compromise that needs the auth log and auditd history searched for the exposure window, not just a config line that gets quietly flipped
Because finding 3 only affects Windows servers, which fall under a stricter SLA than Linux servers
Because finding 1 can be fixed without any CVSS prioritization at all
Because finding 3 is actually less severe than finding 1 and can be deferred indefinitely
Because finding 3 doesn't map to any chapter covered earlier in the course
Because WSUS cannot be used to track Linux patch compliance
questions.explain: Lesson 31 explicitly treats the root-SSH/password-auth finding as a potential compromise rather than a simple misconfiguration — before the sshd_config fix goes in, the auth log and auditd history get searched for root logins during the exposure window, and anything suspicious escalates it to an incident using Chapter 7's endpoint protection tools.
questions.distractorExplain: Option E is wrong on its face — Lesson 31 is explicit that each of the three findings maps directly to a chapter the course already covered (SSH hardening is Lesson 19, fail2ban is Lesson 20), and the case study's entire point is applying that existing knowledge under a deadline, not surfacing anything new.
